sources.news_title: Floods bring rare relief to US Southwest reservoirs as Lake Powell rises 20 feet
sources.text:
- Floods in the U.S. Southwest provide relief to reservoirs amid a megadrought.
- Lake Powell rose over 20 feet, yet remains just over a quarter full.
- El Niño's impact may boost water supplies, but drought conditions persist in the region.
PHOENIX — Recent flooding across the U.S. Southwest is providing rare relief to thirsty reservoirs that had fallen to record lows amid a yearslong megadrought.
Storms in late October and early November sent torrents of water through normally small or dry creeks that overflowed their banks and flooded local communities.
Hundreds of people were told to evacuate, and the flooding cut off access to some areas. Yet most of that water will end up feeding depleted lakes and underground aquifers, said Martin Hoerling, a climate scientist and hydrologist at the University of Colorado, Boulder.
"That's somewhat of an unexpected boost from Mother Nature," Hoerling said.
Last winter's lackluster snowfall did little to recharge water bodies when it melted in the spring and summer, when they typically get their biggest bump of the year.
Then came the chaotic climate phenomenon, El Niño, that has intensified heavy rain and floods. Experts say its impacts will last several more months, potentially further boosting water supplies across the West where water primarily is stored in lakes, aquifers and snowpack.
Lake Powell, the second-largest reservoir in the U.S., rose more than 20 feet from its mid-September low — dwarfing its gains from this year's snowmelt, Hoerling said. Still, the lake remained just over a quarter full, and 15 of its 17 boat launches remained unusable as of Friday.
The floodwaters and additional rain could raise the lake along the Arizona-Utah border further, for a total of over 1.2 million acre-feet — enough to support around 4 million average families for a year, Hoerling estimated.
Cities in the region reported some of their wettest weather in decades.
Before storms began dumping about 7 inches of rain around Pagosa Springs, Colorado, in October, more than 10,000 people in the town and surrounding communities were under water restrictions. Restaurants were encouraged to serve water only on request, town manager David Harris said. Those restrictions are now lifted.
"While the storm was destructive, I think there is a silver lining," Harris said. "You're getting a good start to the winter snowpack in the higher elevations."
Upper Lake Mary, which captures spring snowmelt in Northern Arizona and supplies Flagstaff, Arizona, with up to 40% of its water, received more than 3 billion gallons of water since early October, said Flagstaff water production manager Brian Huntzinger.
Storms last weekend dumped the equivalent of more than two years of water into the town's surface water supply and provided a buffer for an operation that depends heavily on underground aquifers, Huntzinger said.
"It's just a great, great thing to see," Huntzinger said. "We might be overflowing at this rate before we see any snow fly."
In central Arizona, heavy floodwaters that trapped people in their homes gushed into streams that feed the Verde River. That prompted water officials to release water from two nearly full dams into the Verde's normally dry stretch in metro Phoenix, said Bo Svoma, the principal meteorologist at the Salt River Project that manages reservoirs on the Salt and Verde rivers.
The region remains in drought despite the intense rains.
And decisions already have been made to divvy up water in the Colorado River basin. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, which manages reservoirs in the West, is unlikely to change its water releases from Lake Powell or other areas until it knows when snowpack has peaked, typically around April, said Jack Schmidt, a Utah State University professor who studies the Colorado River.
Reclamation spokesperson Mary Carlson acknowledged conditions have improved but added "considerable uncertainty remains."
Under the federal plan for managing the Colorado River's Lower Basin, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet annually in the next two years. That is enough to fill over 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions.
Nevada and Arizona are challenging the plan in court.
Some Arizona cities have agreed to fund preliminary work to reduce reliance on the Colorado River by expanding an existing dam on the Verde River to capture runoff from storms, Svoma said.
"We need to figure out how to be resilient in a drier future. And we're not quite there yet," Hoerling said.

sources.news_title: Extreme Flooding in US Southwest May Foreshadow a Disastrous El Niño Winter
sources.text:
The Southwest just got way too much of a good thing. Last weekend, a ferocious storm inundated communities and killed at least four people. Though precipitation is an essential component of Arizona’s desert climate, the state got two or three months’ worth of it in just a few days — far more than human infrastructure could handle all at once. Since September 20, an astonishing 28.84 inches of rain has fallen on Clovis, New Mexico, compared to its historical average of just 3.3 inches.
“This weekend was just adding more on the rough times that those communities in Southwest Colorado and Arizona and Utah and New Mexico have been having recently,” said Russ Schumacher, director of the Colorado Climate Center at Colorado State University, who’s also the state climatologist. “I think the El Niño connection is pretty clear.”
Indeed, that band of warm water in the Pacific could be priming much of the southern United States for a winter of increased precipitation, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook. “Could an event like this have happened in a non-El Niño year?” asked Michael A. Crimmins, a climatologist at the University of Arizona. “It could have, but it would have been a lot harder to pull all of the ingredients together at the same time, and would have been a lot less likely.”
The looming problem this winter is heat, oddly enough. The unfolding El Niño is already the strongest on record, and it could get stronger still in the next few months. Although that amounts to just a handful of extra degrees in the Pacific, it injects a tremendous amount of energy into the atmosphere, scrambling weather the world over. The phenomenon is so influential, in fact, that it has helped cancel hurricanes over in the Atlantic, by messing with winds high up in the atmosphere. Accordingly, this year shattered the record for the latest first hurricane in a season by nearly a month. Normally by this time of year we’d have seen six of these cyclones, but 2026 has still only produced one.
The Southwest, though, gets no such relief from inclement weather. In addition to adding heat to the sky, the warmer waters of El Niño also increase atmospheric moisture. Even beyond the El Niño, temperatures in the Pacific have been running extra hot, which explains why the western part of the ocean has produced 10 hurricanes this season even as the Atlantic has remained quiet. (Overall, more than 90 percent of the excess heat that humans have pumped into the atmosphere has been absorbed by the oceans.)
All this warm water means more moisture for the weather patterns that have been moving into the Southwest over the last month. A separate system in late October, for instance, became one of the most extreme storms in Colorado’s history, pelting higher elevations with up to 8 inches of rain in four days, causing widespread destruction. “It’s just really extreme amounts of water vapor in the atmosphere that have been aimed into the Southwest in each of those storms,” Schumacher said.
This autumn precipitation primed Arizona, Colorado, and other Southwestern states for yet more destruction this past week. For one, rivers were already running high, then ran all the higher. And two, if soils are soaked, a follow-up bout of rain will run off and cause flooding. “We get the second storm, just a little bit after the first one, then everything was primed for even worse flooding this time around,” Schumacher said.
In mountainous terrain, this gets especially dangerous, as the topography funnels rainwater into raging torrents. “If you hike around the Southwest, you’re going to see out-of-place boulders all over the place,” Crimmins said. “Water put it there. Maybe it was 5,000 years ago or something like that, but water moves. We can have really epic flash flooding.”
The one silver lining here is that any increased precipitation from this El Niño could bring drought relief to much of the southern U.S., according to NOAA’s projections. Climate change is not only exacerbating these ongoing dry spells — hotter temperatures also increase evaporation from reservoirs. At the same time, populations are growing in the Southwest, meaning more people demanding more water.
With these factors conspiring, the Colorado River’s two largest reservoirs, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, are approaching the point of collapse. The potential for more rainfall this winter might help fill them, Schumacher said, but it can’t reverse the system’s precipitous decline. “It’s a long way to go to get even back to where we were a year ago,” he said. “Let alone when it was in good condition decades ago.”
The wildcard this year is snowpack: It’s still too early to tell, Schumacher said, how much snow will fall in Colorado. Whereas rainwater flows quickly into rivers, making it harder to store without overwhelming infrastructure — hence all the destructive flooding of late — snowpack slowly releases water as things thaw in the spring. With a record low snowpack earlier this year, Colorado is in desperate need of bountiful flakes in the months ahead.
Water agencies can’t change the weather, but they can at least change how they manage precipitation. Down in Arizona, cities like Tucson have been installing green infrastructure — basically dirt spaces that hydrate native plants — which slow down the flow of water, thus preventing flooding. “There’s really cool and clever ways of thinking about stormwater as a resource,” Crimmins said, “rather than a nuisance.”

sources.news_title: What a 'historic' water surge at Lake Powell means for the people who depend on it
sources.text:
PAIGE, Ariz. — The weekend is underway at Lake Powell in Paige, Arizona — and people are waiting as workers repair the ramp that historic rising water levels overcame.
"Usually, we get our influx of water in the spring with the runoff, and this is kind of more than we had in the spring, I believe. I think we had 16 feet in the last month," said Lisa Romrell with Lake Powell Guide Service.
Meanwhile, over at Glen Canyon Dam, they're watching — from historic lows back in September, to a record rise.
"I keep track of all that stuff — how much water came into Lake Powell, how much it's filling in," said Robert Betenhauser of Hurricane, Utah.
For Betenhauser, it was powerful to see how a deluge of rain and flooding that hurt his community is helping people at Lake Powell produce power and prosper.
"Water and mud was coming down our street," Betenhauser said.
Emergency declared in Hurricane as more than 100 homes and RVS are damaged by floods:
Costly, damaging rain and flooding hours away in southern Utah is now infusing the economy at Lake Powell.
"This long-term problem has been happening significantly since I've been in Arizona, six years — for this to be the capacity and rising is hope for me," said Kyle Storey of Sedona, Arizona.
As the ramp gets fixed above the rising water, the community continues to move forward.
"There's a lot of people who depend on Lake Powell for their business, and we're one of them — the marina, two marinas — all people who depend on lake Powell to make a living," Romrell said.

sources.news_title: The flood is still arriving at Lake Powell: the biggest day since October 22 came after the rain stopped
sources.text:
The flood is still arriving at Lake Powell: the biggest day since October 22 came after the rain stopped
The rain over the San Juan Mountains ended Monday morning. Wednesday, Lake Powell took in 53,300 cubic feet per second, the most water in a single day since October 22 and the second-largest day of the whole fall. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation's daily record put the lake at 3,535.9 feet Wednesday night, 17.6 feet above where it stood on October 1 and 19.3 feet above the record low it set September 15. The lake is now higher than it has been since January 26. Reclamation had not posted Thursday's figures by Friday morning.
The reason is travel time. The water the second storm put into the San Juan at Pagosa Springs and Farmington on Sunday and Monday took two to three days to come down the river and through the San Juan arm of the lake, and Reclamation measures inflow by the rise of the lake itself. One more big day followed. The San Juan near Bluff fell to 20,800 cubic feet per second Wednesday afternoon, rose again to 31,100 on Thursday, and was down to 17,100 and falling fast early Friday, with the gauges above it at Shiprock and the Four Corners back under 8,000. Thursday's inflow to the lake should be the last large one. After that the river is draining.
What five weeks of water did
Since October 1, the first day of the water year, Lake Powell has gained 1.02 million acre-feet, from 5.17 million to 6.19 million, a little more than a quarter of capacity. The 1.6 million acre-feet that flowed in between October 1 and November 4 is the most for that stretch of the calendar in Reclamation's record, which begins in 1963. The old mark was 1.38 million in 2006. October alone ranked second behind 2006, as the Press reported Wednesday. November has started faster still. The first four days brought 316,000 acre-feet, more than twice the 155,000 that opened November 1986, the previous record, and already 62 percent of what an average full November delivers.
Wednesday's inflow of 53,300 cubic feet per second has been matched or beaten on only four other October or November days in 63 years: October 6 and 7 of 2006, October 22 of this year, and a day in October 1972 that was essentially the same. For comparison, the average fall day since 1963 brings the lake about 8,800.
The water came mostly down the San Juan. The Bluff gauge averaged about 29,800 cubic feet per second on Tuesday. The Colorado River near Cisco, which carries the main stem out of Colorado, crested at 17,700 late Monday night and averaged 15,600 Tuesday, and the Dolores added about 6,000. The Green River, which drains Wyoming and the Uinta Mountains and missed both storms, ran 4,700 to 7,600. Add them up and about 56,000 cubic feet per second was headed for the lake on Tuesday. It arrived Wednesday.
The water Navajo kept
The second flood would have been larger at the lake if Navajo Reservoir had not caught it. Navajo took in 195,000 acre-feet between Sunday and Tuesday, more than 100,000 of it on Monday alone, while the dam released about 260 cubic feet per second. The reservoir rose 17 feet in four days and is now about 81 percent full, with 1.37 million acre-feet, against 67 percent at the end of October. That water is not lost to Lake Powell. It will come down the San Juan next year on Reclamation's schedule instead of in a wall of water this week, which is what the dam was built for.
McPhee Reservoir on the Dolores gained 38,000 acre-feet in four days and Vallecito 16,000. Both are also holding water that would otherwise be at Lake Powell now.
Lake Mead
Lake Mead stood at 1,039.3 feet Wednesday, 2.1 feet above the record low of 1,037.16 it set October 22. Glen Canyon Dam has released a steady 6,500 to 6,700 cubic feet per second all fall, and Hoover Dam released 7,700 Wednesday, so Mead is gaining slowly on the small difference. None of the flood water reaches Mead. It stays behind Glen Canyon Dam unless Reclamation changes the release, which it has not.
What this does and does not change
Reclamation's October 24-Month Study, written before either flood, projected Lake Powell at 3,518.3 feet at the end of December. The lake passed that mark on October 2 and is 17.6 feet above it with eight weeks of the year left. The November study, due about November 13, will be the first to count both floods, and the first that could revise the release range for the water year, which the October study set at 6.0 to 7.0 million acre-feet. Those are the numbers that decide how much water reaches Lake Mead, Arizona, Nevada and California in 2027.
What the floods did not change is the size of the hole. At 3,535.9 feet the lake is 164 feet below full and 46 feet above the elevation at which Glen Canyon Dam can no longer generate power. The 1.6 million acre-feet of the past five weeks is 17 percent of what an average water year brought the lake from 1991 to 2020, 9.5 million acre-feet by Reclamation's own daily record. It is also more than a third of everything the lake received in the water year that ended September 30, which was 4.46 million, less than half of average. The spring runoff that supplies most of a normal year depends on snow that has not fallen yet. The storm that crossed Colorado Wednesday night was forecast by the National Weather Service to put 4 to 8 inches on the central mountains above 10,000 feet, and the week ahead is dry and warm. Whatever snow fell drains to Lake Powell too, in April and May.
Reclamation's daily figures for Lake Powell are at usbr.gov. All of them are provisional. The Press's earlier reports on the lake are here and here.

sources.news_title: The first atmospheric river of Super El Niño is coming
sources.text:
SACRAMENTO — The weather is dry for the moment, but signs across the atmosphere are painting a clear picture for when the first atmospheric river will bring rain to California.
As El Niño begins to lock into the atmosphere, it will continue to set up patterns like the one we will see next week, with lower pressure just offshore and a lingering dome of high pressure across the central United States.
Patterns like this that hold in place for a week or more are exceptional at squeezing out oceanic moisture in the form of atmospheric rivers – strings of the jet stream that become saturated with relentless rain. And the first of the season for Central California is taking shape for next week.
Several atmospheric rivers likely in mid-November
The next seven or so days look quite dry. A stable atmosphere overhead will make for a wonderful week of high temperatures in the upper 60s and low 70s across most of the Golden State.
The trouble comes when this stability moves east. With low pressure already spinning away in the Gulf of Alaska, any stable atmosphere that moves east will pull that Gulf of Alaska low south, where it will quickly be saturated with extra moisture from El Niño and form an atmospheric river.
It is too early to say which day these long-lasting rains could ring out over California, but the probable window is approximately Nov. 11-16, with rain likely only lasting for a day or two.
Atmospheric river rains can be substantial, especially with extra fuel to work with thanks to El Niño. Many areas could quickly see a month's worth of rain in just a few days.
Early projections show Sacramento could receive its entire November rain average — nearly two inches — in the short window. Other areas statewide could see similar numbers, with a general trend for more rain falling in Northern California.
It’s not just rainfall. An early look at what this would mean for Sierra snow shows several feet in placesr. Some Tahoe area resorts are already set to open early, and this should put the rest in a good position to join them.
This is a setup that will grow increasingly common into winter. El Niño is still set to strengthen for another month or two. During that time, don’t be surprised if it feels like these rain events begin to occur on a nearly weekly basis by January.

sources.news_title: ‘Quite a disaster’: Southwest cities struggle to recover after flooding
sources.text:
‘Quite a disaster’: Southwest cities struggle to recover after flooding — PHOTOS
PAGOSA SPRINGS, Colo. — While floodwaters from almost two weeks of on-and-off heavy rain still inundated parts of the U.S. Southwest, other areas left mud-caked by receding torrents presented homeowners and businessowners with the filthy work of cleanup.
Jack Ellis, a retired schoolteacher, surveyed damage along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, which has suffered through multiple rounds of severe flooding in recent weeks.
“This is quite a disaster for everybody, especially in the low-lying areas,” Ellis said. “We dig in and dig out, and that’s what it’s going to take.”
In all, more than 20 trillion gallons of rain — 10 months of the flow over Niagara Falls — have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue.
After rain atop rain, flood risk persists
The U.S. Southwest has endured two recent major rounds of storms, with rain falling on ground already saturated from an especially wet fall.
One person died in floodwaters, and police suspect a second death was weather-related.
Skies were clearing after some rivers crested at levels lower than forecasted, offering a measure of relief to areas that were bracing for more catastrophic flooding, including Shiprock and Farmington in northwestern New Mexico. Devin Neeley, a spokesperson for San Juan County, New Mexico, said major rivers in the area remained above flood stage.
“Now it’s a waiting game for the waters to recede,” Neeley said, adding that the county would likely soon lift evacuation orders impacting at least 20,000 residents and begin to focus on recovery.
Some communities in Colorado and Utah, too, had to make alternative Election Day voting plans because of the flooding.
Another blow for Colorado hot-springs tourist town
An eighth-generation Pagosa Springs local, Gallegos said her ancestors went through a catastrophic flood in 1911 but no one alive in her family expected anything like it in their lifetimes.
She was watching videos of the devastation on social media Monday when she spotted her stepfather’s home swept off its foundation by raging floodwaters. Inside, she knew, were old photographs and other treasured possessions from her childhood.
“My heart’s crushed,” Gallegos said. “And it’s not just him, it’s all the people.”
Cleanup and repairs could take weeks or more in Pagosa Springs, a tourist town famous for hotels with riverside hot springs.
The downtown area remained closed to traffic Tuesday while workers used heavy equipment to clear mud, water and debris from roads.
Walkways and bridges collapsed or were heavily damaged. Outside a resort entrance stacked with sandbags, a sign read “Love Pagosa.”
Basement becomes ‘soup bowl’ in Durango
In Durango, about 60 miles to the west, Willow Bradner’s ranch-style home was surrounded by about 2 feet of mud. Nearly 5 feet of water from an overflowing creek poured inside at one point.
“Our basement became a soup bowl,” she said.
The basement had been a selling point when she bought the property in 2024. Bradner said she and her husband once asked if they needed flood insurance and were told they were not in a flood zone.
They and their teenage daughter had been offered a place to stay through the end of the year. But the loss of their home and uncertainty about the future were overwhelming, Bradner said.
“The majority of our savings is in this house,” she said. “We have to dig deep, and we have to rebuild.”
— Peters reported from Santa Fe, New Mexico, and Gruver from Fort Collins, Colorado. Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed.

sources.news_title: The Super El Niño is already soaking the U.S. Expect more flooding to come
sources.text:
A house floating down the San Juan River in Colorado, crumbling as it crashes into a bridge. A man evacuated from a palm tree surrounded by floodwaters in Brevard County, Florida. These are scenes from the “Super El Niño”–fueled rain events that are now soaking parts of the U.S.
This week the Southwest’s Four Corners region and Florida’s central coast have experienced major flood events, swamping homes and washing out roads. It was impossible to reach meteorologists in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, by phone on Tuesday because a major fiber cable in town had been cut by flooding, bringing down cell service.
Arleen Prochazka, a retired Air Force meteorologist who co-runs the nonprofit Pagosa Weather, managed to speak with Scientific American by email Wednesday.

“Homes were standing essentially in lakes,” she says. Back-to-back storms have made recovery difficult, she adds. “Most roads have deep potholes and are very rutted along the edges that flowed with water, mud and debris. Many roads are still impassable.”
And it’s not just the U.S.—in recent weeks Ecuador and Peru have experienced extreme soaking rains and floods, driven by the strong El Niño and what Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, calls “absurd” ocean warming.
“We are seeing the hydroclimate effects of a very strong El Niño event occurring now but with a boost from climate change,” Swain says.
El Niño typically brings moisture-laden air to the desert Southwest in autumn. The climate pattern also boosts precipitation in Florida from fall to spring. In that sense, these events are precisely what would be expected, given the strength of the current El Niño.
Even so, the rainfall has been historic. In Malabar, Fla., two feet of rain fell in 36 hours over November 1 and November 2, according to the National Weather Service. It was a once-in-1,000-year event for the region, meaning that there is only a one-in-1,000 chance of such an extreme rainstorm in that area in a given year. One meteorologist estimated that 1.9 trillion gallons of water fell across Florida in 24 hours.
In the Four Corners region, which spans Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona, this week’s rainfall came on top of storms that, a little more than a week ago, dumped 100-year to 1,000-year levels of rainfall on parts of all four states. Flooding along the San Juan River during that event pushed the river’s crest to 15 feet. This week flows went even higher, with a river peak at 16.81 feet in the town of Pagosa Springs, Colo. The damage comes only a year after intense October 2025 flooding, driven by the remnants of Pacific cyclones.
“Getting essentially three of these big rainstorms in two years is very unusual,” says Russ Schumacher, a meteorologist at Colorado State University and Colorado’s state climatologist.
El Niño conditions provide a favorable jet stream for these autumn storms, Swain says, but this year’s event is supercharged by a marine heat wave off the West Coast of Central and North America. “Off the coast of Baja California, the water is 11 or 12 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than average,” he says. “That is astonishing.”
Ocean temperatures are also high in the Atlantic near Florida, he says, providing local storms with a “mind-boggling amount of moisture to work with.”
The NWS Climate Prediction Center forecasts a strong to very strong El Niño from January to March 2027. Florida will likely experience a winter of severe thunderstorms, Swain says, while the risk of flooding in the U.S. West will shift to California over the next few weeks.

sources.news_title: Lake Powell dead pool fears ease slightly
sources.text:
Lake Powell has risen following heavy rains, providing a slight, if perhaps only temporary ease to concerns that dwindling water levels were threatening hydropower production at Glen Canyon Dam.
The nation’s second-largest reservoir fell to record low levels in September. However, recent heavy rainfall in the Southwest has offered some reprieve. Water levels at the reservoir, which straddles the Arizona-Utah border, have risen from a mid-September low of around 3,519 feet to approximately 3,537 feet as of Wednesday, according to provisional U.S. Geological Survey data.
A spokesperson for the Bureau of Reclamation, which manages the reservoir, previously indicated to Newsweek the agency expected the rise. Following earlier stormy conditions, they said: "Recent precipitation has significantly improved inflows to Lake Powell, and, with additional storms forecast through the end of the month, reservoir elevations could rise further."
Read More on News
The agency told Newsweek on Wednesday: "The recent heavy precipitation in parts of the Colorado River Basin has improved many near-term reservoir conditions, but it is very early in the forecasting season, and considerable uncertainty remains. Reclamation continues to plan for a range of future hydrologic conditions and prepare for a wide range of operational scenarios."
Downstream, Lake Mead—America’s largest reservoir—saw relatively little improvement. Levels as of Wednesday were largely unchanged compared with mid-September, according to Reclamation data. Lake Mead’s water level is also affected by releases from Lake Powell.
The agency’s spokesperson previously said, however, that the reservoir was expected to end October and November about three feet higher than projections previously indicated.
"Precipitation in the Lower Colorado Basin has resulted in additional tributary inflow into Lake Mead as well as less water demand from the irrigation districts in southern Arizona and California," they said at the time.
While the region’s storms appear to have been good news for Lake Powell, they led to damaging floods and forced evacuations in portions of the Southwest, including Colorado and Arizona.
The flooding also disrupted Election Day plans on Tuesday. Roads and bridges were washed out; polling locations such as Rock Point, Arizona, flooded; and some ballots were swept away, preventing or delaying voters from reaching polling stations.
Hydropower Concerns Persist Amid Long-Term Drought
Though Lake Powell’s levels have seen an uptick, the Colorado River system in which it is situated has been grappling with a multidecadal drought, the effects of which experts say a single event can’t reverse.
Reclamation warned earlier this year that the reservoir’s water levels faced falling to below 3,490 feet—the minimum level needed for hydropower production—"without major intervention." The agency announced steps to prevent this, including increased releases from Flaming Gorge Reservoir upstream and a cut in downstream releases to Lake Mead.
"The recent, and continuing, rise of Lake Powell is significant, in the sense that we have taken a half-step back from the edge of the cliff. Powell has returned to conditions in early February 2026. But those conditions were a true crisis," Jack Schmidt, a senior research scientist at the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University told Newsweek. "Taking a full step back from the edge of the class can only come if we have a huge winter of Rocky Mountain snow. and even then we will remain perilously close to the cliff edge."
Mike Crimmins, climate science extension specialist at the University of Arizona, told KTAR in Arizona on Friday, ahead of the most recent downpours: "It’s going to put off dead pool for a little bit, right? We were getting dangerously low to that issue with Lake Powell. So, this actually creates a little bit more margin."
Crimmins said that. while short-term drought conditions would improve, long-term drought remains.
"Water resources are different when you have droughts accumulate over years to many years. You really can’t just erase those deficits in a couple of weeks," he said.
Sarah Porter, director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University told Newsweek: "We need much more water to flow into the reservoir to ease concerns, much less stabilize the system."
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Tobias Meyjes and James Debens

sources.news_title: Deadly Floods Swamp Southwest, Forcing Hundreds To Evacuate
sources.text:
The skies were clearing, but the risk of flooding remained over parts of the U.S. Southwest after powerful downpours sent massive amounts of water surging over the usually dry landscape, forcing hundreds to evacuate and keeping swift-water rescue teams busy.
Officials said cleanup and repair efforts could take weeks. One person died in the floodwaters and police suspect a second death was weather-related.
The National Weather Service said Monday that isolated cloudbursts were still possible across the Four Corners region — where New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah meet — as the phenomenon stoked by warming Pacific waters known as El Niño disrupts weather patterns.
Damage was widespread in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town of about 2,000. Officials feared the San Juan River that flows through it would top a level that nearly wiped out the town in 1911. The river reached 16.81 feet (5.1 meters) Sunday — a foot lower than the historic level — flooding downtown streets before receding Monday, the weather service said.
An entire home was lifted from its foundation and floated down the river before crashing into a pedestrian bridge. A section of a road bridge west of town crumbled under raging waters, said Archuleta County Sheriff’s Office spokesperson Vicki Shaffer.
Dozens of people were rescued across the region, including some by helicopter. Shaffer said first responders were searching for people who may be stranded.
“That will continue, just like last week, until we’re sure that everybody who was trapped by the floodwaters has been rescued,” she said.
The Colorado Department of Transportation reopened several closed bridges and roadways late Monday. Shaffer said evacuation orders remain in place, though she wasn’t sure how many people were affected.
Pagosa Springs had just lifted an evacuation order from a previous storm, only to reimpose it Saturday.
More than 20 trillion gallons of rain have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to calculations by former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue.
With Election Day coming, officials in Colorado and Utah arranged alternative voting plans for evacuated or stranded residents.
Utah said Monday that residents of hard-hit San Juan County will be allowed to vote electronically because some of them may not be able to reach polling places.
More rivers rise, forcing evacuations
Evacuations were ordered along the San Juan River in New Mexico, which officials warned was still rising and could crest Tuesday through Wednesday. The village of Chama, New Mexico, was also evacuated and cut off by road closures.
Residents had to leave their homes along the Animas River in southwestern Colorado, where Durango police Chief Brice Current said authorities were checking Monday on those who rode out the flooding at home.
“There’s still a lot of people stranded,” Current said.
Willow Bradner and her family have been staying in a hotel since their Durango home flooded this weekend.
“We went from ‘we’re going to be safe’ to ‘pack a go-bag’ in 45 minutes,” she recalled. Her basement is now filled with water, with the house surrounded by more than 2 feet (60 centimeters) of mud.
On Monday, Greg Ewing was among some 200 community members who used shovels and skid steers to remove the mud in Bradner’s neighborhood. “That’s the cool thing about Durango. It’s a really strong community. Everyone comes together,” Ewing said.
Dry Arizona creek beds turned to raging torrents
Record rainfall was reported across Arizona, including 7.3 inches (18.5 centimeters) over two days at Workman Creek, a wilderness area near Phoenix.
Flagstaff totaled 5.15 inches (13 centimeters) over two days, contributing to its wettest Nov. 1 ever recorded. The city typically has fewer than a handful of days per year of rain exceeding 1 inch (2.5 centimeters), said meteorologist Jennifer Tate with the NWS Weather Prediction Center.
“What really stood out to me was that this wasn’t localized. It was a very broad system that brought a lot of rain to a lot of places,” Tate said.
A man was seen falling into floodwaters rushing into a drainage tunnel in Flagstaff, where rain fell nearly nonstop Sunday. Police said the body of Williams Singavarapu, 73, of New York, was discovered Monday about 15 blocks from where he disappeared.
A second man was found dead Monday in a drainage area, Flagstaff police said, adding it appeared to be weather-related, pending an official determination on the cause of death.
In Sedona, floodwaters trapped several people in their homes, and heavy rain washed out part of a highway.
Nearby in Camp Verde, Doug Michaels was cooking dinner at an RV park when he saw people evacuating as water rose. He was able to get himself, his wife, cat and valuables to safety and raise his camper higher off the ground. But he said others fared much worse.
“It’s devastating,” he said. “People lost their homes. The one lady doesn’t even know where her camper is. It went down the river.”
Swift-water rescues also were conducted in Tucson, where weather service meteorologist Aaron Hardin said “we are getting two or three months of rain in a span of a couple of days.”
Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs issued a statewide emergency declaration on Monday after recently issuing an emergency for Navajo and Coconino counties. The governors of New Mexico and Colorado asked President Donald Trump to declare a major disaster to receive federal funding assistance.
Swaths of southern Utah are inundated
Ryan Benally spent the weekend building dirt berms to divert floodwaters from his parents’ home on the Navajo Nation near Montezuma Creek, Utah. So far, the barriers have held, though parts of their small cattle ranch were under water.
Benally, an assistant professor at Utah State University, has been coordinating deliveries of bottled water, waterproof boots, toiletries and other supplies to shelters. Families who stayed at home were increasingly difficult to reach, he said, because access routes for some remote residents washed out.
Benally said his parents, both in their 60s, have lived in the area all their lives and have never seen flooding this severe.
“These storms have been one after another after another,” Benally said. “It’s compounding in ways people out here just weren’t prepared for.”
___
AP journalists Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; Sarah Raza in Sioux Falls, South Dakota; Savannah Peters in Santa Fe, New Mexico; Gregory Bull in Durango, Colorado; Ross D. Franklin in Camp Verde, Arizona; and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed.

sources.news_title: Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse?
sources.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A chaotic climate phenomenon is intensifying heavy rains and floods in the Southwest, experts say.
A natural warming cycle called El Niño is sizzling Pacific Ocean waters, leaking moisture into the air that can fuel passing storms. Such El Niño events can happen irregularly every couple of years, but scientists say the latest iteration is particularly extreme — and it’s just getting started, with impacts expected for several more months.
“We’ve had super El Niños in the past, but this is a super duper El Niño,” said meteorologist Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections.
The phenomenon wasn’t the only cause of the severe storms and it’s difficult to attribute any single event to it. Still, scientists say this supercharged El Niño is making heavy rains more likely and intense across the Southern U.S. The effects of those storms can be felt more strongly in desert regions, where the land doesn’t absorb water as well.
Flash floods on Sunday prompted evacuations across northern New Mexico and central Arizona, and a Colorado ski town braced for its main river to rise to catastrophic levels. And just last week, another soaker of a storm subjected southwestern states to days of flooding.
Over 20 trillion gallons of water have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to calculations by former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue.
Experts say this year’s extreme El Niño is creating more ideal conditions for storms. It’s adding more moisture to the air, which is perfect fodder for downpours to draw upon. And it’s shifting wind patterns across the globe, redirecting strong air currents toward the Southwest that can stir up that moisture.
“The likelihood of big precipitation in the Southwest interior does go up this time of year, but we’re seeing it to a degree we actually haven’t seen before,” said climate scientist Daniel Swain with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources.
This El Niño is sloshing warmer waters into new places, but the world’s oceans are already hotter than they used to be because of human-caused climate change. That means even more sweltering extremes are possible.
“The fact that the ocean temperatures are already warmer than they were, say, 100 years ago, makes these El Niño situations even more intense,” said meteorologist Randy Cerveny with Arizona State University.
The phenomenon is changing weather patterns around the world: regions including Peru and Ecuador are also seeing record-breaking flooding, Swain said. Parts of Southeast Asia, like Indonesia, are drier than usual.
The El Niño event is expected to peak in December, when it can more strongly harness certain air currents called jet streams to produce more extreme storms across the western U.S. After that, experts say its onslaught could continue for months.
“The dice are certainly loaded for more heavy storms this winter and spring,” said Park Williams with UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography in an email.
The impacts of an El Niño aren’t wholly bad, Cerveny said: it can bring rainfall and moisture to drier areas like the Southwest and fill up reservoirs. At the same time, storms and floods can pose a danger to people and property.
To stay safe, experts recommended watching the forecast, planning ahead and heeding evacuation warnings from local authorities.
“We’re not at the peak of the heating in the Pacific Ocean. So yes, we will see more of these particular events,” Cerveny said.
__

sources.news_title: Extreme flooding in the Southwest foreshadows a wild #ElNiño winter — Matt Simon (Grist.org) #ENSO
sources.text:
Click the link to read the article on the Grist website (Matt Simon):
November 5, 2026
The Southwest just got way too much of a good thing. Last weekend, a ferocious storm inundated communities and killed at least four people. Though precipitation is an essential component of Arizona’s desert climate, the state got two or three months’ worth of it in just a few days — far more than human infrastructure could handle all at once. Since September 20, an astonishing 28.84 inches of rain has fallen on Clovis, New Mexico, compared to its historical average of just 3.3 inches.
“This weekend was just adding more on the rough times that those communities in Southwest Colorado and Arizona and Utah and New Mexico have been having recently,” said Russ Schumacher, director of the Colorado Climate Center at Colorado State University, who’s also the state climatologist. “I think the El Niño connection is pretty clear.”
Indeed, that band of warm water in the Pacific could be priming much of the southern United States for a winter of increased precipitation, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook. “Could an event like this have happened in a non-El Niño year?” asked Michael A. Crimmins, a climatologist at the University of Arizona. “It could have, but it would have been a lot harder to pull all of the ingredients together at the same time, and would have been a lot less likely.”
The looming problem this winter is heat, oddly enough. The unfolding El Niño is already the strongest on record, and it could get stronger still in the next few months. Although that amounts to just a handful of extra degrees in the Pacific, it injects a tremendous amount of energy into the atmosphere, scrambling weather the world over. The phenomenon is so influential, in fact, that it has helped cancel hurricanes over in the Atlantic, by messing with winds high up in the atmosphere. Accordingly, this year shattered the recordfor the latest first hurricane in a season by nearly a month. Normally by this time of year we’d have seen six of these cyclones, but 2026 has still only produced one.
The Southwest, though, gets no such relief from inclement weather. In addition to adding heat to the sky, the warmer waters of El Niño also increase atmospheric moisture. Even beyond the El Niño, temperatures in the Pacific have been running extra hot, which explains why the western part of the ocean has produced 10 hurricanes this season even as the Atlantic has remained quiet. (Overall, more than 90 percent of the excess heat that humans have pumped into the atmosphere has been absorbed by the oceans.)
All this warm water means more moisture for the weather patterns that have been moving into the Southwest over the last month. A separate system in late October, for instance, became one of the most extreme storms in Colorado’s history, pelting higher elevations with up to 8 inches of rain in four days, causing widespread destruction. “It’s just really extreme amounts of water vapor in the atmosphere that have been aimed into the Southwest in each of those storms,” Schumacher said.
This autumn precipitation primed Arizona, Colorado, and other Southwestern states for yet more destruction this past week. For one, rivers were already running high, then ran all the higher. And two, if soils are soaked, a follow-up bout of rain will run off and cause flooding. “We get the second storm, just a little bit after the first one, then everything was primed for even worse flooding this time around,” Schumacher said.
In mountainous terrain, this gets especially dangerous, as the topography funnels rainwater into raging torrents. “If you hike around the Southwest, you’re going to see out-of-place boulders all over the place,” Crimmins said. “Water put it there. Maybe it was 5,000 years ago or something like that, but water moves. We can have really epic flash flooding.”
The one silver lining here is that any increased precipitation from this El Niño could bring drought relief to much of the southern U.S., according to NOAA’s projections. Climate change is not only exacerbating these ongoing dry spells — hotter temperatures also increase evaporation from reservoirs. At the same time, populations are growing in the Southwest, meaning more people demanding more water.
With these factors conspiring, the Colorado River’s two largest reservoirs, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, are approaching the point of collapse. The potential for more rainfall this winter might help fill them, Schumacher said, but it can’t reverse the system’s precipitous decline. “It’s a long way to go to get even back to where we were a year ago,” he said. “Let alone when it was in good condition decades ago.”
The wildcard this year is snowpack: It’s still too early to tell, Schumacher said, how much snow will fall in Colorado. Whereas rainwater flows quickly into rivers, making it harder to store without overwhelming infrastructure — hence all the destructive flooding of late — snowpack slowly releases water as things thaw in the spring. With a record low snowpack earlier this year, Colorado is in desperate need of bountiful flakes in the months ahead.
Water agencies can’t change the weather, but they can at least change how they manage precipitation. Down in Arizona, cities like Tucson have been installing green infrastructure — basically dirt spaces that hydrate native plants — which slow down the flow of water, thus preventing flooding. “There’s really cool and clever ways of thinking about stormwater as a resource,” Crimmins said, “rather than a nuisance.”
